writing.prompt: Directions: For this part, you are allowed 30 minutes to write a short essay based on the picture below. You should focus on the difficulty in acquiring useful information in spite of advanced information technology. You are required to write at least 150 words but no more than 200 words.
writing.sample: The picture presents a thought-provoking scene: five people are gathered around a long table for a meeting, four of them staring at their computer screens, while a standing man remarks, "We have lots of information technology. We just don't have much useful information." Simple as it is, the drawing points to a striking paradox of our digital age.What the cartoon truly reveals is that advanced technology does not automatically bring valuable knowledge. On the contrary, several factors make useful information hard to obtain. First, the sheer information overload buries genuine insights under mountains of trivial data. Second, true and false messages are so mixed together that few can discern which sources are authentic. Moreover, fragmented reading weakens our ability to sift through and process what really matters.Therefore, we should not be dazzled by shiny gadgets alone. What truly counts is the capacity to filter, evaluate and apply information wisely. Only by cultivating critical thinking and selective attention can we turn an ocean of raw data into genuine understanding.

transcript.en: W: One of the most interesting experiments with dolphins must be one done by Doctor Jarvis Bastian. What he tried to do was to teach a male dolphin called Buss and a female called Doris to communicate with each other across a solid barrier.
transcript.zh: W: 关于海豚最有趣的实验之一，应该就是贾维斯·巴斯蒂安博士所做的那个实验。他试图教一只名叫 Buss 的雄性海豚和一只名叫 Doris 的雌性海豚隔着一道坚固的屏障相互交流。

transcript.en: M: So how did he do it exactly?
transcript.zh: M: 那他具体是怎么做的呢？

transcript.en: W: Well, first of all, he kept the two dolphins together in the same tank and taught them to press levers whenever they saw a light. The levers were fitted to the side of the tank next to each other. If the light flashed on and off several times, the dolphins were supposed to press the left-hand lever followed by the right-hand one. If the light was kept steady, the dolphins were supposed to press the levers in reverse order. Whenever they responded correctly, they were rewarded with fish.
transcript.zh: W: 首先，他把两只海豚养在同一个水箱里，并教它们每当看到灯光时就按下杠杆。杠杆安装在水箱侧面，彼此相邻。如果灯光反复闪烁几次，海豚就应该先按左边的杠杆，再按右边的杠杆。如果灯光一直保持稳定，海豚就应该按相反的顺序按下杠杆。每当它们作出正确反应时，就会得到鱼作为奖励。

transcript.en: M: Sounds terribly complicated.
transcript.zh: M: 听起来复杂得不得了。

transcript.en: W: Well, that was the first stage. In the second stage, Doctor Bastian separated the dolphins into two tanks. They could still hear one another, but they couldn't actually see each other. The levers and the light were set up in exactly the same way except that this time it was only Doris who could see the light indicating which lever to press first. But in order to get their fish, both dolphins had to press the levers in the correct order. This meant of course that Doris had to tell Buss whether it was a flashing light or whether it was a steady light.
transcript.zh: W: 嗯，那是第一阶段。第二阶段，巴斯蒂安博士把两只海豚分别关在两个水箱里。它们仍然能听见彼此的声音，但实际上看不见对方。杠杆和灯光的设置完全相同，只是这一次，只有 Doris 能看到指示先按哪个杠杆的灯光。但为了得到鱼，两只海豚都必须按正确的顺序按下杠杆。这当然意味着 Doris 必须告诉 Buss，灯光是在闪烁，还是一直保持稳定。

transcript.en: M: So did it work?
transcript.zh: M: 那成功了吗？

transcript.en: W: Well, amazingly enough, the dolphins achieved a 100% success rate.
transcript.zh: W: 嗯，令人惊讶的是，这两只海豚达到了百分之百的成功率。

transcript.en: W: This week's program "Up Your Street" takes you to Harrogate, a small town in Yorkshire. Harrogate became a fashionable resort during Victorian times, when people came to take a bath in the mineral waters. Today, few people come to visit the town for its mineral waters. Instead, Harrogate has become a popular town for people to retire to. Its clean air, attractive parks, and the absence of any industry, make this an ideal spot for people looking for a quiet life. Now, to tell us more about Harrogate, I have with me Tom Percival, President of the Chamber of Commerce. Tom, one of the things a visitor notices about Harrogate is the large area of open parkland right down into the middle of the town. Can you tell us more about it?
transcript.zh: W: 本周的《街头巷尾》节目带大家走进约克郡的小镇哈罗盖特。在维多利亚时代，人们纷纷来到这里泡矿泉，哈罗盖特也因而成为时尚的度假胜地。如今，很少有人为了矿泉造访这座小镇了。相反，哈罗盖特成为了一个备受欢迎的退休养老小镇。这里空气清新，公园宜人，没有任何工业，是追求宁静生活的人们的理想去处。现在，为了让我们进一步了解哈罗盖特，我们请到了商会会长汤姆·珀西瓦尔。汤姆，游客注意到哈罗盖特的其中一点，就是有一大片开阔的公园绿地一直延伸到镇中心。你能给我们多讲讲吗？

transcript.en: M: Yes, certainly. The area is called the Stray.
transcript.zh: M: 好的，没问题。这片区域叫做“斯特雷”。

transcript.en: W: Why the Stray?
transcript.zh: W: 为什么叫“斯特雷”？

transcript.en: M: It's called that because in the old days, people let their cattle stray on the area, which was common land.
transcript.zh: M: 叫这个名字是因为在过去，这片土地是公地，人们会让他们的牛群在上面漫游。

transcript.en: W: Oh, I see.
transcript.zh: W: 哦，我明白了。

transcript.en: M: Then, with changes in farming and in land ownership, the Stray became part of the land owned by Harrogate.
transcript.zh: M: 后来，随着农业和土地所有权的变化，“斯特雷”成为了哈罗盖特所有土地的一部分。

transcript.en: W: And is it protected?
transcript.zh: W: 那它受到保护吗？

transcript.en: M: Oh, yes, indeed. There's a special law: no one can build anything on the Stray. It's protected forever.
transcript.zh: M: 哦，是的，确实受到了保护。有一项专门的法律：任何人都不能在“斯特雷”上建造任何东西。它得到了永久保护。

transcript.en: W: So it'll always be parkland?
transcript.zh: W: 所以它会一直是公园绿地？

transcript.en: M: That's right. As you can see, some of the Stray is used for sports fields.
transcript.zh: M: 没错。正如你所看到的，“斯特雷”的一部分被用作运动场地。

transcript.en: W: I believe it looks lovely in the spring.
transcript.zh: W: 我想它在春天看起来一定很漂亮。

transcript.en: M: Yes, it does. There're spring flowers on the old trees, and people visit the town just to see the flowers.
transcript.zh: M: 是的，确实很漂亮。老树上开满了春花，人们造访这座小镇就是为了来看花。

transcript.en: Russell Fazio, an Ohio State psychology professor who has studied interracial roommates there and at Indiana University, discovered an intriguing academic effect. In a study analyzing data on thousands of Ohio State freshmen who lived in dorms, he found the black freshmen who came to college with high standardized test scores earned better grades if they had a white roommate even if the roommate's test scores were low. The roommate's race had no effect on the grades of white students or low-scoring black students. Perhaps, the study speculated, having a white roommate helps academically prepared black students adjust to a predominantly white university.
transcript.zh: 俄亥俄州立大学心理学教授罗素·法齐奥曾在该校和印第安纳大学研究不同种族的室友关系，并发现了一种耐人寻味的学术效应。在一项分析数千名居住在宿舍的俄亥俄州立大学新生数据的研究中，他发现，那些带着较高标准化考试成绩进入大学的黑人新生，如果与一名白人学生同住，即使对方的考试成绩较低，他们也能取得更好的成绩。室友的种族对成绩较好的白人学生或考试成绩较低的黑人学生没有影响。该研究推测，也许拥有一名白人室友有助于学业准备充分的黑人学生适应一所以白人为主的大学。

transcript.en: That same study found the randomly assigned interracial roommates at Ohio State broke up before the end of the quarter about twice as often as same-race roommates. Because interracial roommate relationships are often problematic, Dr. Fazio said, many students would like to move out, but university housing policies may make it hard to leave. "At Indiana University, where housing was not so tight, more interracial roommates split up," he said. "Here at Ohio State, where housing was tight, they were told to work it out. The most interesting thing we found was that if the relationship managed to continue for just 10 weeks, we could see an improvement in racial attitudes."
transcript.zh: 同一项研究发现，在俄亥俄州立大学，随机分配的跨种族室友在学期结束前分开的情况约为同种族室友的两倍。法齐奥博士说，由于跨种族室友关系往往存在问题，许多学生希望搬出去，但大学的住宿政策可能使他们难以离开。他说：“在住宿安排没有那么紧张的印第安纳大学，更多跨种族室友选择分开。在住宿紧张的俄亥俄州立大学，学校要求他们设法解决问题。我们发现的最有意思的事情是，如果这段关系能够仅仅持续十周，我们就能看到他们的种族态度有所改善。”

transcript.en: Dr. Fazio's Indiana study found that three times as many randomly assigned interracial roommates were no longer living together at the end of the semester, compared with white roommates. The interracial roommates spent less time together, and had fewer joint activities than the white pairs.
transcript.zh: 法齐奥博士在印第安纳大学开展的研究发现，与白人室友相比，随机分配的跨种族室友在学期结束时不再共同居住的比例是前者的三倍。跨种族室友共处的时间更少，开展的共同活动也少于白人室友组合。

transcript.en: In a small laboratory at the Medical University of South Carolina, Dr. Vladimir Mironov has been working for a decade to grow meat. A developmental biologist and tissue engineer, Dr. Mironov is one of only a few scientists worldwide involved in bioengineering "cultured" meat. It's a product he believes could help solve future global food crises resulting from shrinking amounts of land available for growing meat the old-fashioned way. "Growth of cultured meat is also under way in the Netherlands," Mironov told Reuters in an interview, "but in the United States, it is science in search of funding and demand."
transcript.zh: 在南卡罗来纳医科大学的一间小型实验室里，弗拉基米尔·米罗诺夫博士十年来一直致力于培育肉类。作为一名发育生物学家和组织工程师，米罗诺夫博士是全球仅有的少数参与生物工程“培养肉”研究的科学家之一。他相信，这种产品或许有助于解决未来全球粮食危机，而这场危机源于可用来以传统方式生产肉类的土地日益减少。“培养肉的培育工作在荷兰也正在进行，”米罗诺夫在接受路透社采访时说，“但在美国，这项科学还在寻找资金和市场需求。”

transcript.en: The new National Institute of Food and Agriculture won't fund it, the National Institute of Health won't fund it, and NASA funded it only briefly, Mironov said. "It's classic disruptive technology," Mironov said. "Bringing any new technology on the market, on average, costs $1 billion. We don't even have $1 million."
transcript.zh: 米罗诺夫说，新成立的国家食品与农业研究所不会为这项研究提供资金，国立卫生研究院也不会提供资金，而美国国家航空航天局只提供了很短时间的资助。“这是一项典型的颠覆性技术，”米罗诺夫说，“将任何新技术推向市场，平均需要10亿美元。我们连100万美元都没有。”

transcript.en: Director of the Advanced Tissue Biofabrication Center in the Department of Regenerative Medicine and Cell Biology at the medical university, Mironov now primarily conducts research on tissue engineering, or growing, of human organs. "There's an unpleasant factor when people find out meat is grown in a lab. They don't like to associate technology with food," said Nicholas Genovese, a visiting scholar in cancer cell biology. "But there are a lot of products that we eat today that are considered natural that are produced in a similar manner," Genovese said.
transcript.zh: 米罗诺夫是该医科大学再生医学与细胞生物学系先进组织生物制造中心的主任，目前主要开展组织工程研究，即研究人类器官的培育。“当人们发现肉是在实验室里培育出来的时，会产生一种不适感。他们不喜欢把技术与食物联系在一起，”癌症细胞生物学访问学者尼古拉斯·杰诺维斯说。“但如今我们食用的许多被认为是天然的产品，实际上也是以类似的方式生产出来的，”杰诺维斯说。

Questions 19 to 22 are based on the recording you have just heard.

transcript.en: Moderator:
transcript.zh: 主持人：

transcript.en: Good morning, everybody. It is my pleasure to introduce our speaker for today's lecture, Dr. Howard Walcott. Dr. Walcott has written numerous articles on the topic of stress management. Today he will talk about how to deal with stress and pressure. Welcome, Dr. Walcott.
transcript.zh: 大家早上好。很荣幸向大家介绍今天讲座的演讲者霍华德·沃尔科特博士。沃尔科特博士曾撰写大量关于压力管理的文章。今天，他将谈谈如何应对压力和心理负担。欢迎您，沃尔科特博士。

transcript.en: Dr. Walcott:
transcript.zh: 沃尔科特博士：

transcript.en: Hello, everyone. Today's lecture will focus on how to fight against stress.
transcript.zh: 大家好。今天的讲座将重点讨论如何对抗压力。

transcript.en: Every human being experiences stress in life. Our tiring jobs, faulty eating habits and pollution may add to the cause of stress. Everyone reacts to stress differently. Some can cope with it and some cannot. Studies have proved that an increase in stress hormones might speed up cognitive decline in people as you age.
transcript.zh: 每个人在生活中都会经历压力。劳累的工作、不良的饮食习惯和污染都可能加剧压力的产生。每个人对压力的反应各不相同。有些人能够应对压力，而有些人则不能。研究证明，随着年龄增长，压力激素水平的升高可能会加速人的认知能力衰退。

transcript.en: When you feel stress, your body produces chemicals which lead to an increase in blood pressure, high blood sugar levels and in the worst case may lead to major organ damage. So, it is important to fight against stress before it troubles you.
transcript.zh: 当你感到压力时，身体会产生一些化学物质，导致血压升高、血糖水平升高，最严重的情况下还可能造成主要器官损伤。因此，在压力给你带来困扰之前，及时对抗压力十分重要。

transcript.en: Here are some of the most effective natural stress reducers:
transcript.zh: 以下是一些最有效的天然减压方法：

transcript.en: Music therapy: How about a prescription for ear soothing music to fight and overcome stress and diseases? Sounds great, doesn't it? Whether you accept it or not, music affects our daily life, as every human responds to it. A combination of psychology and counselling, music can act as a healing therapy to cure several conditions like depression, personality issues, cancer, etc.
transcript.zh: 音乐疗法：用舒缓悦耳的音乐来对抗和克服压力及疾病，怎么样？听起来很不错，不是吗？无论你是否接受这一点，音乐都会影响我们的日常生活，因为每个人都会对音乐产生反应。音乐结合了心理学和咨询，可以作为一种治疗手段，帮助治愈抑郁症、人格问题、癌症等多种病症。

transcript.en: Outdoor walking: Walking is an inexpensive, low-risk and the easiest accessible form of exercise. It significantly contributes to enhanced mental and physical health.
transcript.zh: 户外步行：步行是一种费用低、风险小且最容易进行的运动形式。它对改善身心健康有显著作用。

transcript.en: Meditation: Meditation is certainly the best way to keep stress at bay. As studies suggest, daily 25 minutes of focused meditation drastically affects people's ability to recover under stress.
transcript.zh: 冥想：冥想无疑是远离压力的最佳方式。研究表明，每天进行25分钟专注的冥想，会显著影响人们在压力下的恢复能力。

transcript.en: Massage: If you are a massage lover, here is one more reason for you to indulge in it more often as massage improves vascular function and helps in reducing stress. Essential oils help to soothe your mind and eliminate anxiety.
transcript.zh: 按摩：如果你喜欢按摩，那么这里还有一个让你更经常享受按摩的理由，因为按摩能够改善血管功能，并有助于减轻压力。精油有助于舒缓心情、消除焦虑。

transcript.en: Sleep well: Most of us do not care about our sleeping schedule or do not get adequate sleep. A good amount of sleep of say 7-8 hours is a must to relax your mind and reduce stress levels.
transcript.zh: 保证良好睡眠：我们大多数人并不在意自己的睡眠时间安排，或者无法获得充足的睡眠。每天保证足够的睡眠，比如7至8小时，对于放松身心和降低压力水平是必不可少的。

transcript.en: Exercise: Studies have proved that daily physical exercise helps protect your brain from stress-induced depression. One should ensure physical activity like walking, jogging, playing games like tennis or football on a daily basis for at least 30 minutes as it is very good for one's mind.
transcript.zh: 锻炼：研究证明，每天进行体育锻炼有助于保护大脑免受压力导致的抑郁影响。每天至少进行30分钟的体育活动，例如步行、慢跑，或打网球、踢足球等，对人的心理健康非常有益。

transcript.en: Positive thinking: Yes, you heard it right. Positive thinking plays a major role in combating stress. It may be a little difficult to think positively in a stressful situation, but believe it or not giving positive messages to your mind helps ease anxiety and helps you remain calm and happy.
transcript.zh: 积极思考：是的，你没有听错。积极思考在对抗压力方面发挥着重要作用。在充满压力的情况下保持积极思考可能有些困难，但信不信由你，给自己的内心传递积极的信息有助于缓解焦虑，并帮助你保持平静和愉快。

transcript.en: Laugh out loud and smile: No, I am not kidding. "Laughter is the best medicine" is an age-old saying and holds true in this age too. Whenever you face a situation when you are extremely stressed, try laughing or if not at least smile as it releases chemicals which decrease stress level in the body. I hope the lecture today will be of help and benefit to you. Thank you.
transcript.zh: 大声笑出来并保持微笑：不，我不是在开玩笑。“笑是最好的良药”是一句流传已久的谚语，在今天仍然适用。每当你遇到极度紧张的情况时，试着笑出来，至少也要微笑，因为这样会释放出能够降低体内压力水平的化学物质。希望今天的讲座能对你有所帮助并让你受益。谢谢。

transcript.en: Hello, everyone. Last time we talked about the history of television. Today, I'd like to talk about the roles television has been playing in Americans' political life.
transcript.zh: 大家好。上次我们谈到了电视的历史。今天，我想谈谈电视在美国人政治生活中所发挥的作用。

transcript.en: Television has transformed politics in the United States by changing the way in which information is spread, by altering political campaigns, and by changing citizens' patterns of response to politics. By giving citizens independent access to the candidates, television diminished the role of the political party in the selection of the major party candidates. By centering politics on the person of the candidate, television accelerated the citizens' focus on character rather than issues.
transcript.zh: 电视通过改变信息传播的方式、改变政治竞选活动，以及改变公民对政治的反应模式，改变了美国的政治。由于让公民能够独立接触候选人，电视削弱了政党在主要政党候选人遴选中的作用。由于将政治的中心置于候选人本人身上，电视加速了公民对个人品格而非政治议题的关注。

transcript.en: Television has altered the forms of political communication as well. The messages on which most of us rely are briefer than they once were. The stump speech, a political speech given by travelling politicians and lasting hours, which characterized nineteenth-century political discourse, has given way to the 30-second advertisement and the 10-second sound bite in broadcast news. Increasingly the audience for speeches is not that standing in front of the politician but rather the viewing audience who will hear and see a part of the speech on the news.
transcript.zh: 电视也改变了政治传播的形式。我们大多数人所依赖的信息，比过去更加简短。19世纪政治话语的典型形式是竞选巡回演说，即政治家在各地巡回发表、持续数小时的政治演讲；如今，这种演说已让位于广播新闻中的30秒广告和10秒片段。演讲的听众越来越不再是站在政治家面前的那些人，而是通过新闻听到并看到演讲部分内容的电视观众。

transcript.en: In these abbreviated forms, much of what constituted the traditional political discourse of earlier ages has been lost. In 15 or 30 seconds, a speaker cannot establish the historical context that shaped the issue in question, cannot detail the probable causes of the problem, and cannot examine alternative proposals to argue that one is preferable to others. Politicians assert but do not argue.
transcript.zh: 在这些简略的形式中，早期时代传统政治话语所包含的许多内容都丧失了。在15秒或30秒内，演讲者无法说明塑造相关议题的历史背景，无法详细阐述问题可能产生的原因，也无法考察各种替代方案，以论证其中一种优于其他方案。政治家只作断言，却不进行论证。

transcript.en: Because television is an intimate medium, speaking through it requires a changed political style that is more conversational, personal, and visual than that of the old-style stump speech. Reliance on television means that increasingly our political world contains memorable pictures rather than memorable words. Schools teach us to analyze words and print. However, in a world in which politics is increasingly visual, informed citizenship requires a new set of skills.
transcript.zh: 由于电视是一种具有亲密感的媒介，通过电视讲话需要一种不同的政治风格，这种风格比老式竞选巡回演说更具会话性、个人色彩和视觉性。依赖电视意味着，我们的政治世界中越来越多的是令人难忘的画面，而不是令人难忘的言语。学校教我们分析文字和印刷材料。然而，在政治日益视觉化的世界里，成为知情公民需要一套新的技能。

transcript.en: Recognizing the power of television's pictures, politicians craft televisual, staged events, called pseudo-events, designed to attract media coverage. Much of the political activity we see on television news has been crafted by politicians, their speechwriters, and their public relations advisers for televised consumption. Sound bites in news and answers to questions in debates increasingly sound like advertisements.
transcript.zh: 认识到电视画面的力量后，政治家们精心策划电视化的现场活动，即所谓的“伪事件”，以吸引媒体报道。我们在电视新闻中看到的许多政治活动，都是政治家、他们的演讲稿撰写人和公共关系顾问为电视播出而策划的。新闻中的简短引语以及辩论中的问题回答，听起来越来越像广告。

transcript.en: A survey is a study, generally in the form of an interview or a questionnaire that provides information concerning how people think and act. In the United States, the best-known surveys are the Gallup poll and the Harris poll. As anyone who watches the news during presidential campaigns knows, these polls have become an important part of political life in the United States.
transcript.zh: 调查是一项研究，通常采用访谈或问卷的形式，用于了解人们的想法和行为。在美国，最为人熟知的调查是盖洛普民意测验和哈里斯民意测验。正如任何在总统竞选期间观看新闻的人所知道的那样，这些民意测验已经成为美国政治生活的重要组成部分。

transcript.en: North Americans are familiar with the many person-on-the-street interviews on local television news shows. While such interviews can be highly entertaining, they are not necessarily an accurate indication of public opinion. First, they reflect the opinions of only those people who appear at a certain location. Thus, such samples can be biased in favour of commuters, middle-class shoppers, or factory workers, depending on which area the news people select. Second, television interviews tend to attract outgoing people who are willing to appear on the air, while they frighten away others who may feel intimidated by a camera. A survey must be based on a precise, representative sampling if it is to genuinely reflect a broad range of the population.
transcript.zh: 北美人对地方电视新闻节目中众多的街头采访并不陌生。虽然这类采访可能非常有趣，但未必能准确反映公众舆论。首先，它们只反映出现在某一特定地点的人的意见。因此，根据新闻工作者选择的区域不同，这类样本可能偏向于通勤者、中产阶级购物者或工厂工人。其次，电视采访往往会吸引那些性格外向、愿意出现在电视节目中的人，同时会吓退另一些可能因摄像机而感到拘谨的人。调查若要真正反映社会各阶层的广泛情况，就必须建立在精确且具有代表性的抽样基础上。

transcript.en: In preparing to conduct a survey, sociologists must exercise great care in the wording of questions. An effective survey question must be simple and clear enough for people to understand it. It must also be specific enough so that there are no problems in interpreting the results. Even questions that are less structured must be carefully phrased in order to elicit the type of information desired. Surveys can become indispensable sources of information, but only if the sampling is done properly and the questions are worded accurately.
transcript.zh: 在准备开展调查时，社会学家必须非常谨慎地斟酌问题的措辞。有效的调查问题必须足够简单、清晰，使人们能够理解。问题还必须足够具体，以免在解释结果时产生困难。即使是结构较为松散的问题，也必须经过仔细措辞，才能获取所需要的那类信息。调查可以成为不可或缺的信息来源，但前提是抽样得当，问题措辞准确。

transcript.en: There are two main forms of surveys: the interview and the questionnaire. Each of these forms of survey research has its advantages. An interviewer can obtain a high response rate because people find it more difficult to turn down a personal request for an interview than to throw away a written questionnaire. In addition, an interviewer can go beyond written questions and probe for a subject's underlying feelings and reasons. However, questionnaires have the advantage of being cheaper and more consistent.
transcript.zh: 调查主要有两种形式：访谈和问卷。这两种调查研究形式各有其优点。访谈者能够获得较高的回应率，因为相比于丢弃一份书面问卷，人们更难拒绝面对面的访谈请求。此外，访谈者可以超越书面问题，进一步探究受访者内心的感受及其原因。然而，问卷的优点在于成本更低，而且更加一致。

matching.title: How do we convince our inner caveman to be greener? We ask some outstanding social scientists.

paragraphs.t: The road to climate hell is paved with our good intentions. Politicians may tackle polluters while scientists do battle with carbon emissions. But the most pervasive problem is less obvious: our own behaviour. We get distracted before we can turn down the heating. We break our promise not to fly after hearing about a neighbour's trip to India. Ultimately, we can't be bothered to change our attitude. Fortunately for the planet, social science and behavioural economics may be able to do that for us.

Despite mournful polar bears and charts showing carbon emissions soaring, most people find it hard to believe that global warming will affect them personally. Recent polls by the Pew Research Centre in Washington, DC, found that 75-80 percent of participants regarded climate change as an important issue. But respondents ranked it last on a list of priorities.

This inconsistency largely stems from a feeling of powerlessness. "When we can't actually remove the source of our fear, we tend to adapt psychologically by adopting a range of defense mechanisms," says Tom Crompton, change strategist for the environmental organization World Wide Fund for Nature.

Part of the fault lies with our inner caveman. Evolution has programmed humans to pay most attention to issues that will have an immediate impact. "We worry most about now because if we don't survive for the next minute, we're not going to be around in ten years' time," says Professor Elke Weber of the Centre for Research on Environmental Decisions at Columbia University in New York. If the Thames were lapping around Big Ben, Londoners would face up to the problem of emissions pretty quickly. But in practice, our brain discounts the risks—and benefits—associated with issues that lie some way ahead.

Matthew Rush worth, of the Department of Experimental Psychology at the University of Oxford, sees this in his lab every day. "One of the ways in which all agents seem to make decisions is that they assign a lower weighting to outcomes that are going to be further away in the future," he says. "This is a very sensible way for an animal to make decisions in the wild and would have been very helpful for humans for thousands of years."

Not any longer. By the time we wake up to the threat posed by climate change, it could well be too late. And if we're not going to make rational decisions about the future, others may have to help us to do so.

Few political libraries are without a copy of Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth and Happiness, by Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein. They argue that governments should persuade us into making better decisions—such as saving more in our pension plans—by changing the default options. Professor Weber believes that environmental policy can make use of similar tactics. If, for example, building codes included green construction guidelines, most developers would be too lazy to challenge them.

Defaults are certainly part of the solution. But social scientists are most concerned about crafting messages that exploit our group mentality(心态). "We need to understand what motivates people, what it is that allows them to make change," says Professor Neil Adger, of the Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research in Norwich. "It is actually about what their peers think of them, what their social norms are, what is seen as desirable in society." In other words, our inner caveman is continually looking over his shoulder to see what the rest of the tribe are up to.

The passive attitude we have to climate change as individuals can be altered by counting us in—and measuring us against—our peer group. "Social norms are primitive and elemental," says Dr. Robert Cialdini, author of Influence: The Psychology of Persuasion. "Birds flock together, fish school together, cattle herd together…" just perceiving norms is enough to cause people to adjust their behavior in the direction of the crowd.

These norms can take us beyond good intentions. Cialdini conducted a study in San Diego in which coat hangers bearing messages about saving energy were hung on people's doors. Some of the messages mentioned the environment, some financial savings, others social responsibility. But it was the ones that mentioned the actions of neighbours that drove down power use.

Other studies show that simply providing the facility for people to compare their energy use with the local average is enough to cause them to modify their behaviour. The Conservatives plan to adopt this strategy by making utility companies print the average local electricity and gas usage on people's bills.

Social science can also teach politicians how to avoid our collective capacity for self-destructive behaviour. Environmental campaigns that tell us how many people drive SUVs unwittingly(不经意地) imply that this behaviour is widespread and thus permissible. Cialdini recommends some careful framing of the message. "Instead of normalising the undesirable behaviour, the message needs to marginalise it, for example, by stating that if even one person buys yet another SUV, it reduces our ability to be energy-independent."

Tapping into how we already see ourselves is crucial. The most successful environmental strategy will marry the green message to our own sense of identity. Take your average trade union member, chances are they will be politically motivated and be used to collective action—much like Erica Gregory. A retired member of the Public and Commercial Services Union, she is setting up one of 1,100 action groups with the support of Climate Solidarity, a two-year environmental campaign aimed at trade unionists.

Erica is proof that a great-grandmother can help to lead the revolution if you get the psychology right—in this case, by matching her enthusiasm for the environment with a fondness for organising groups. "I think it's a terrific idea," she says of the campaign. "The union backing it makes members think there must be something in it." She is expecting up to 20 people at the first meeting she has called, at her local pub in the Cornish village of Polperro.

Nick Perks, project director for Climate Solidarity, believes this sort of activity is where the future of environmental action lies. "Using existing civil society structures or networks is a more effective way of creating change… and obviously trade unions are one of the biggest civil society networks in the UK," he says. The "Love Food, Hate Waste" campaign entered into a collaboration last year with another such network—the Women's Institute. Londoner Rachel Taylor joined the campaign with the aim of making new friends. A year on, the meetings have made lasting changes to what she throws away in her kitchen. "It's always more of an incentive if you're doing it with other people," she says. "It motivates you more if you know that you've got to provide feedback to a group."

The power of such simple psychology in fighting climate change is attracting attention across the political establishment. In the US, the House of Representatives Science Committee has approved a bill allocating $10 million a year to studying energy-related behaviour. In the UK, new studies are in development and social scientists are regularly spotted in British government offices. With the help of psychologists, there is fresh hope that we might go green after all.

One study shows that our neighbours' actions are influential in changing our behaviour.

We should take our future into consideration in making decisions concerning climate change before it is too late.

careful.passage: More than a decade ago, cognitive scientists John Bransford and Daniel Schwartz, both then at Vanderbilt University, found that what distinguished young adults from children was not the ability to retain facts or apply prior knowledge to a new situation but a quality they called "preparation for future learning." The researchers asked fifth graders and college students to create a recovery plan to protect bald eagles from extinction. Shockingly, the two groups came up with plans of similar quality (though the college students had better spelling skills). From the standpoint of a traditional educator, this outcome indicated that schooling had failed to help students think about ecosystems and extinction, major scientific ideas. The researchers decided to go deeper, however. They asked both groups to generate questions about important issues needed to create recovery plans. On this task, they found large differences. College students focused on critical issues of interdependence between eagles and their habitat(栖息地). Fifth graders tended to focus on features of individual eagles ("How big are they?" and "What do they eat?"). The college students had cultivated the ability to ask questions, the cornerstone of critical thinking. They had learned how to learn. Museums and other institutions of informal learning may be better suited to teach this skill than elementary and secondary schools. At the Exploratorium in San Francisco, we recently studied how learning to ask good questions can affect the quality of people's scientific inquiry. We found that when we taught participants to ask "What if?" and "How can?" questions that nobody present would know the answer to and that would spark exploration, they engaged in better inquiry at the next exhibit—asking more questions, performing more experiments and making better interpretations of their results. Specifically, their questions became more comprehensive at the new exhibit. Rather than merely asking about something they wanted to try, they tended to include both cause and effect in their question. Asking juicy questions appears to be a transferable skill for deepening collaborative inquiry into the science content found in exhibits. This type of learning is not confined to museums or institutional settings. Informal learning environment tolerates failure better than schools. Perhaps many teachers have too little time to allow students to form and pursue their own questions and too much ground to cover in the curriculum. But people must acquire this skill somewhere. Our society depends on them being able to make critical decisions about their own medical treatment, say, or what we must do about global energy needs and demands. For that, we have a robust informal system that gives no grades, takes all comers, and is available even on holidays and weekends.

careful.passage: "There's an old saying in the space world: amateurs talk about technology, professionals talk about insurance." In an interview last year with The Economist, George Whitesides, chief executive of space-tourism firm Virgin Galactic, was placing his company in the latter category. But insurance will be cold comfort following the failure on October 31st of VSS Enterprise, resulting in the death of one pilot and the severe injury to another. On top of the tragic loss of life, the accident in California will cast a long shadow over the future of space tourism, even before it has properly begun. The notion of space tourism took hold in 2001 with a $20 million flight aboard a Russian spacecraft by Dennis Tito, a millionaire engineer with an adventurous streak. Just half a dozen holiday-makers have reached orbit since then, for similarly astronomical price tags. But more recently, companies have begun to plan more affordable "suborbital" flights—briefer ventures just to the edge of space's vast darkness. Virgin Galactic had, prior to this week's accident, seemed closest to starting regular flights. The company has already taken deposits from around 800 would-be space tourists, including Stephen Hawking. After being dogged by technical delays for years, Sir Richard Branson, Virgin Galactic's founder, had recently suggested that a SpaceShipTwo craft would carry its first paying customers as soon as February 2015. That now seems an impossible timeline. In July, a sister craft of the crashed spaceplane was reported to be about half-finished. The other half will have to wait, as authorities of America's Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) and National Transportation Safety Board work out what went wrong. In the meantime, the entire space tourism industry will be on tenterhooks(坐立不安). The 2004 Commercial Space Launch Amendments Act, intended to encourage private space vehicles and services, prohibits the transportation secretary (and thereby the FAA) from regulating the design or operation of private spacecraft, unless they have resulted in a serious or fatal injury to crew or passengers. That means that the FAA could suspend Virgin Galactic's license to fly. It could also insist on checking private manned spacecraft as thoroughly as it does commercial aircraft. While that may make suborbital travel safer, it would add significant cost and complexity to an emerging industry that has until now operated largely as the playground of billionaires and dreamy engineers. How Virgin Galactic, regulators and the public respond to this most recent tragedy will determine whether and how soon private space travel can transcend that playground. There is no doubt that spaceflight entails risks, and to pioneer a new mode of travel is to free those risks, and to reduce them with the benefit of hard-won experience.

translation.source: 最近，中国政府决定将其工业升级。中国现在涉足建造高速列车、远洋船舶、机器人，甚至飞机。不久 前，中国获得了在印度尼西亚(Indonesia)建造一条高铁的合同;中国还与马来西亚(Malaysia)签署了为其提供高 速列车的合同。这证明人们信赖中国造产品。 中国造产品越来越受欢迎。中国为此付出了代价,但这确实有助 于消除贫困，同时还为世界各地的人们提供了就业机会。这是一件好事，值得称赞。下次你去商店时,可能想 看一看你所购商品的出产国名。很有可能这件商品是中国造的。
translation.reference: Recently, the Chinese government decided to upgrade its industries. China is now engaged in building high-speed trains, ocean-going ships, robots and even airplanes. Not long ago, China won the contract to build a high-speed railway in Indonesia; it also signed a contract with Malaysia to provide it with high-speed trains. This proves that people trust products made in China. Products made in China are becoming more and more popular. China has paid a price for this, but it does help eliminate poverty and also provides employment for people around the world. This is a good thing worthy of praise. The next time you go to a store, you may want to take a look at the country of origin of the goods you buy. It is very likely that this product is made in China.
